ed-wound-ortho-l01.q: A dog bite wound is being sent home on antibiotics. Which agent is appropriate and why does cephalexin alone fall short?
choices: Amoxicillin-clavulanate, because it covers Pasteurella, Eikenella and anaerobes that a cephalosporin alone misses
Cephalexin alone, because it already covers Pasteurella species
Clindamycin alone, because it is the narrowest agent that still covers the bite flora
No antibiotic is needed for a dog bite unless it becomes infected
ed-wound-ortho-l01.why: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the standard because it covers Pasteurella, Eikenella and oral anaerobes in one agent. Cephalexin alone does not reliably cover Pasteurella, so it under-treats the wound even though it looks like reasonable empiric skin coverage. Clindamycin has gaps against some of the same organisms. Bites are contaminated wounds with high infection rates, so prophylaxis is standard, not something reserved for wounds that already look infected.

ed-wound-ortho-l01.q: A worker's forearm was pinned briefly under a pallet. The skin shows only mild abrasion and looks far less alarming than the mechanism. What should be suspected?
choices: Nothing further; superficial skin findings mean the injury is minor
A crush injury, where the tissue underneath may be dead despite intact-looking skin, with risk of high infection and compartment syndrome
A clenched-fist fight bite, since any hand or arm trauma should be treated that way
A high-pressure injection injury requiring immediate hand surgery consultation
ed-wound-ortho-l01.why: Crush wounds are dangerous precisely because the skin can look nearly normal while the tissue beneath is dead, so the visible injury under-represents the real damage. This carries high infection risk, poor healing, and a real risk of compartment syndrome, which is why crush mechanism itself is a red flag regardless of surface appearance. A fight bite requires a knuckle-to-tooth mechanism, and high-pressure injection requires a pressurized tool, neither of which fits a pallet crush.

ed-wound-ortho-l02.q: What is considered normal two-point discrimination at an uninjured fingertip, and why does the exam compare it to the other hand?
choices: Under 6 mm, and the uninjured side is tested for a baseline because normal sensation varies between people
Under 15 mm, and comparison is only needed in children
Under 2 mm, and comparison is optional since the number is fixed for all patients
There is no numeric standard; the test is purely subjective
ed-wound-ortho-l02.why: Normal two-point discrimination at a fingertip is under 6 mm, and testing the uninjured side gives a personal baseline since exact thresholds vary slightly between individuals. A 15 mm or purely subjective standard would miss real nerve injury, and 2 mm is tighter than the accepted normal, which would falsely flag normal fingers as abnormal.

ed-wound-ortho-l02.q: A contaminated hand laceration is closed primarily to save the patient a follow-up visit. What is the risk of this decision, and what should have happened instead?
choices: There is no added risk; closure always speeds healing regardless of contamination
Closing it converts an open, drainable problem into a closed abscess; it should have been packed open or left for delayed closure with a recheck
The risk is only cosmetic scarring, which is an acceptable tradeoff for convenience
The wound should have been closed with tissue adhesive instead of sutures to reduce infection risk
ed-wound-ortho-l02.why: Closing an infected or heavily contaminated wound seals bacteria in and converts a drainable open wound into a closed abscess, which is more dangerous than the open wound was. The correct move is delayed primary closure or leaving it open with a scheduled recheck. Adhesive does not solve the contamination problem since it is still sealing the wound; the risk is infectious, not just cosmetic.

ed-wound-ortho-l03.q: A 6 cm laceration needs irrigation before repair. Using the standard rule of thumb, roughly how much irrigant is needed and at what pressure?
choices: About 10 to 20 mL total, poured gently from a bottle
Roughly 300 to 600 mL, delivered at 5 to 8 psi using a syringe with a splash shield or 19 gauge needle
About 1 mL per cm, at whatever pressure a wall-mounted tap provides
Exactly 1 L regardless of wound length, delivered at high pressure to sterilize the wound
ed-wound-ortho-l03.why: The rule of thumb is roughly 50 to 100 mL per centimeter of wound length, so a 6 cm wound needs on the order of 300 to 600 mL, delivered at 5 to 8 psi from a syringe with a splash shield or a 19 gauge needle. Pouring from a bottle does not generate the pressure needed to mechanically clean the wound, and a fixed 1 L regardless of length ignores wound size; irrigation reduces bioburden, it does not sterilize.

ed-wound-ortho-l03.q: A clinician plans tissue adhesive to close a 2 cm laceration directly over a knuckle that must keep bending. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: Nothing; adhesive is ideal for any small, linear wound regardless of location
Adhesive should be avoided over joints because motion breaks the bond, and it needs a low-tension wound whose edges already meet
Adhesive is contraindicated because it is too toxic to use near joints
The wound is too short for adhesive; only wounds over 5 cm can be closed this way
ed-wound-ortho-l03.why: Tissue adhesive is meant for short, clean, linear, low-tension wounds whose edges already sit together, and it is specifically avoided over joints because ongoing motion breaks the bond before it can hold. It is not a toxicity issue, and wound length is not the limiting factor here — motion and tension are. Adhesive actually suits short wounds, not long ones.

ed-wound-ortho-l04.q: A simple abscess with a cavity under about 5 cm is drained. Current practice regarding packing this cavity is best described as which of the following?
choices: Packing is mandatory in every abscess regardless of size to prevent premature closure
Packing a cavity this size is no longer automatic; it increases pain without clear benefit, and loop drainage is a common alternative
Packing is never appropriate for any abscess and has been fully abandoned
Packing is required only if the patient has a fever at the time of drainage
ed-wound-ortho-l04.why: For cavities under about 5 cm, routine packing is no longer automatic care since it adds pain without a clear benefit, and loop drainage is now a common alternative — though this varies by protocol. It has not been fully abandoned for larger or more complex cavities, and fever is not the deciding factor for whether to pack; the deciding factor is cavity size and clinical judgment.

ed-wound-ortho-l04.q: A patient describes a tender, swollen area on the thigh that he assumed was a spider bite, though he never saw anything bite him. What does this presentation most often represent, and how should it change the antibiotic choice if purulent?
choices: A true spider bite; standard cephalexin is appropriate
An MRSA abscess or purulent infection; empiric coverage should include TMP-SMX, doxycycline or clindamycin rather than cephalexin alone
A normal insect bite that needs no antibiotics at all
Cellulitis from strep, so cephalexin is the correct choice
ed-wound-ortho-l04.why: A self-described 'spider bite' that the patient never actually witnessed is a classic description for an MRSA skin infection. Purulent presentations should prompt MRSA-active coverage such as TMP-SMX, doxycycline or clindamycin instead of a plain cephalosporin, which covers streptococcus well but not MRSA. Dismissing it as a harmless bite or treating it as simple strep cellulitis both under-treat the likely pathogen.

ed-wound-ortho-l05.q: Cool running water is applied to a fresh burn. Up to how long after the burn does this cooling remain effective, and what should never be used instead?
choices: Up to 3 hours after the burn; ice should never be used because it worsens injury and can drop core temperature
Only within the first 2 minutes; after that cooling does nothing
Up to 24 hours after the burn; ice is preferred over water for large burns
There is no time limit, and ice is the fastest way to cool a burn
ed-wound-ortho-l05.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes remains effective up to 3 hours after the injury. Ice is never used because it causes further tissue injury and can drop core temperature, especially in large burns. Claiming a 2-minute window is far too short given the documented 3-hour benefit, and claiming no time limit or preferring ice both contradict standard burn first aid.

ed-wound-ortho-l05.q: Silver sulfadiazine is being considered for a burn dressing. In which situation should it be avoided?
choices: In a superficial partial-thickness burn on the forearm of a healthy adult
In a facial burn, a patient with sulfa allergy, a pregnant patient, or an infant under 2 months
In any burn larger than 10% of body surface area
In burns caused by scalding rather than flame
ed-wound-ortho-l05.why: Silver sulfadiazine is avoided on the face, in sulfa allergy, in pregnancy, and in infants under 2 months. An adult forearm burn with no contraindication is a reasonable use; burn size and whether the mechanism was scald versus flame are not the factors that rule it out — the contraindications are tied to the patient and the anatomic site, not the burn's size or cause.

ed-wound-ortho-l06.q: A patient with a humeral shaft fracture is splinted before anyone checks wrist extension. Roughly how often does this fracture injure the radial nerve, and what should have happened first?
choices: About 10 to 18%; wrist extension and first web space sensation should be documented before splinting
Under 1%; no special nerve check is needed for this fracture
About 50%; the patient should go straight to surgery before any splint is applied
The radial nerve is not at risk in humeral shaft fractures, only the median nerve is
ed-wound-ortho-l06.why: The radial nerve runs in a groove along the back of the humeral shaft and is injured in roughly 10 to 18% of these fractures, producing wrist drop and numbness in the first web space. That deficit must be documented before the splint goes on, because once immobilized it is unclear whether a deficit was pre-existing or caused by the splint. Both the under-1% and 50% figures misstate the real incidence, and the median nerve is not the nerve at risk here.

ed-wound-ortho-l06.q: Two forearm fracture-dislocation patterns are easy to confuse. Which correctly distinguishes Monteggia from Galeazzi?
choices: Monteggia is a proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation; Galeazzi is a distal radius fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption
Monteggia is a distal radius fracture with radial head dislocation; Galeazzi is a proximal ulna fracture with wrist disruption
Both terms describe the same injury pattern at different ages
Monteggia involves only soft tissue; Galeazzi always involves bone
ed-wound-ortho-l06.why: Monteggia pairs a proximal ulna fracture with a dislocated radial head, while Galeazzi pairs a distal radius fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint — near-mirror injuries at opposite ends of the forearm, which is exactly why they are easy to swap. They are not the same injury at different ages, and both are bony injuries with an associated joint disruption, not purely soft tissue.

ed-wound-ortho-l07.q: A patient with an isolated mid-shaft femur fracture is also found to have a fracture of the hip on the same side. What does this mean for traction splint use?
choices: A traction splint is still ideal since it is the standard treatment for any femur fracture
A traction splint is contraindicated because it is only appropriate for an isolated mid-shaft fracture, and pulling traction against an injured hip on that side can worsen the injury
A traction splint should be applied to the opposite, uninjured leg instead
Traction splints are never used for femur fractures under any circumstances
ed-wound-ortho-l07.why: A traction splint is meant for an isolated mid-shaft femur fracture and is contraindicated when there is an associated hip or knee injury on that same side, a pelvic fracture, an ankle or foot injury, or a partial amputation — pulling traction against a co-existing injury can worsen it. Traction splints are a real and standard tool for isolated femur fractures, so ruling them out entirely is wrong, and applying one to the uninjured leg makes no sense.

ed-wound-ortho-l07.q: A patient has severe midfoot pain and bruising across the sole of the foot after a sports injury but a routine standing foot x-ray looks unremarkable. What injury should still be suspected, and what confirms it?
choices: A simple toe fracture; buddy taping is sufficient
A Lisfranc injury; weight-bearing views and widening over 2 mm between the first and second metatarsal bases make it visible
A calcaneus fracture; a lumbar spine film is needed next
A Jones fracture; this requires only a hard-soled shoe
ed-wound-ortho-l07.why: Plantar bruising with midfoot pain out of proportion is a classic but commonly missed sign of a Lisfranc injury, and standard non-weight-bearing films can look deceptively normal. Weight-bearing views revealing more than 2 mm of widening between the first and second metatarsal bases confirms it, and most need surgery. A toe fracture or Jones fracture do not fit the plantar bruising pattern, and a calcaneus fracture comes from axial heel loading, not this mechanism.

ed-wound-ortho-l08.q: When compartment pressures are measured, what delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) indicates the need for fasciotomy?
choices: Under 30 mmHg
Under 5 mmHg
Over 60 mmHg
Delta pressure is not used; only the absolute compartment pressure matters
ed-wound-ortho-l08.why: A delta pressure under 30 mmHg — diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure — indicates fasciotomy is needed, because it means the compartment pressure is close enough to the patient's own perfusion pressure to be strangling the muscle. An under-5 mmHg threshold would miss dangerous compartments long before pressure got that extreme, and delta pressure, not the raw absolute number alone, is the clinically used comparison.

ed-wound-ortho-l08.q: A patient with a tibial shaft fracture has strong distal pulses and a pink foot. Does this rule out compartment syndrome?
choices: Yes, a strong pulse and pink foot effectively rule it out
No, pulses are usually present in compartment syndrome because compartment pressure exceeds small-vessel perfusion pressure long before it reaches arterial pressure
Only in children does pulse presence rule it out
Pulses are irrelevant to the diagnosis and are never checked
ed-wound-ortho-l08.why: Pulses are usually present in compartment syndrome, since the rising compartment pressure exceeds the pressure in small vessels feeding the muscle well before it climbs high enough to occlude the artery itself. Waiting for pulselessness means waiting until the muscle is already dead. Pulses are still checked and documented, just not relied on to exclude the diagnosis, and this logic applies in adults as much as children.

ed-wound-ortho-l09.q: A patient with a posterior hip dislocation is being evaluated. Beyond urgency, what specific nerve must be checked before and after reduction?
choices: The sciatic nerve, by testing foot dorsiflexion and sensation over the top of the foot
The axillary nerve, by testing sensation over the outer deltoid
The radial nerve, by testing wrist extension
The femoral nerve, by testing hip flexion strength
ed-wound-ortho-l09.why: Hip dislocation, especially posterior, places the sciatic nerve at risk, so foot dorsiflexion and sensation over the top of the foot are checked before and after reduction. The axillary nerve is the one checked in shoulder injuries, the radial nerve in humeral shaft fractures, and the femoral nerve is not the nerve typically stressed by a posterior hip dislocation.

ed-wound-ortho-l09.q: A patient on crutches is told to lean their body weight onto the crutch pads under their armpits for stability. What is wrong with this instruction?
choices: Nothing; the armpits are designed to bear crutch weight
Weight should go through the hands, not the armpits, because leaning on the armpits compresses the radial nerve
Weight should go through the armpits only when going up stairs
Crutches should never touch the armpits at all, even for measurement
ed-wound-ortho-l09.why: Crutch weight is meant to go through the hands, with the top pad resting close to but not bearing weight against the armpit, because leaning on the armpits compresses the radial nerve running through that area and can cause a nerve injury. The pads do sit near the armpit for fit and stability, so avoiding contact entirely is impractical — the key instruction is where the weight is borne, not full avoidance of contact.

ed-wound-ortho-l10.q: Which Salter-Harris fracture type is the most common, and roughly what fraction of growth plate fractures does it represent?
choices: Type II, about 75%
Type I, about 75%
Type V, about 50%
Type III, about 90%
ed-wound-ortho-l10.why: Type II, where the fracture line runs through the physis and up into the metaphysis, is the most common pattern and accounts for roughly 75% of growth plate fractures. Type I can look deceptively normal on x-ray but is less common than Type II; Type V is the rarest and carries the worst prognosis rather than being common; Type III enters the joint but is not the majority pattern.

ed-wound-ortho-l10.q: A toddler will not bear weight on one leg after starting to walk, and the initial tibia x-ray is read as normal. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Discharge with reassurance since the x-ray is normal
Immobilize presumptively for a toddler's fracture, since the initial x-ray is frequently negative for this non-displaced spiral tibial crack
Obtain an MRI immediately regardless of exam findings
Assume abuse and file a report without further evaluation
ed-wound-ortho-l10.why: A toddler's fracture is a non-displaced spiral crack of the lower tibia in a child roughly 9 months to 3 years old who has recently started walking, and the x-ray is frequently negative early on, so the child is immobilized anyway based on the clinical picture. Discharging without any plan ignores that pattern, immediate MRI is not the standard first step, and jumping to an abuse report is not supported by a toddler's fracture presentation alone, which is a recognized accidental mechanism.

quiz.q: A patient steps on a rusty nail that punctures through the sole of his sneaker into his foot. Which organism is specifically associated with this mechanism?
choices: Pseudomonas from foam material carried into the wound by the shoe
Clostridium tetani causing immediate infection
Streptococcus pyogenes from skin flora alone
Staphylococcus aureus from the nail itself
quiz.why: A nail through a sneaker classically drives foam and debris from the shoe into the puncture tract, carrying Pseudomonas deep into the foot with a specific risk of osteomyelitis. Staph aureus and strep are common skin-flora infecting organisms generally but are not the organism specifically tied to this mechanism. Tetanus is a toxin-mediated disease, not an infection that appears immediately, and it is prevented by immunization status, not treated as an acute infecting organism.

quiz.q: A patient has an avulsion injury where a flap of skin on the lower leg is torn and hanging, attached only at its distal edge. What does this tell you about the flap's viability?
choices: The flap has excellent blood supply because distal attachment preserves flow
The flap likely has poor blood supply because a distally based flap is worse off than a proximally based one
Flap viability cannot be predicted by its base location
The flap should be fully removed regardless of viability
quiz.why: A flap based distally has worse blood supply than one based proximally, because the vessels supplying skin generally run from proximal to distal, so a flap hinged only at its far end is cut off from its normal inflow. This makes distally based flaps more prone to necrosis. Blood supply is very much predictable from the base location, and viable tissue is preserved rather than automatically removed.

quiz.q: A patient's finger is amputated in a table saw accident. The part is found nearby. What is the correct way to prepare it for transport with the patient?
choices: Place it directly on ice to keep it as cold as possible
Submerge it directly in sterile water
Wrap it in saline-moistened gauze, seal it in a plastic bag, then place the bag on ice water
Wrap it in a dry towel and keep it at room temperature
quiz.why: The amputated part is wrapped in saline-moistened gauze, sealed in a plastic bag, and the bag is placed on ice water, which cools the tissue without freezing it or letting it become waterlogged. Direct ice contact or submersion in water causes frostbite-type injury or maceration of the tissue, and room temperature storage allows ongoing tissue death from ischemia.

quiz.q: A patient was bitten on the forearm by another person during a fight three hours ago. Which combination best describes the concern with human bites?
choices: No specific antibiotic coverage is needed beyond routine wound care
Human bites are treated identically to abrasions with no special concern
Low infection risk and organisms limited to skin flora
High infection risk from Eikenella corrodens and oral anaerobes, with risk of joint and tendon sheath inoculation
quiz.why: Human bites carry a 10 to 25% infection rate driven by Eikenella corrodens and oral anaerobes, and the bite mechanism can inoculate a joint or tendon sheath, which is a much deeper and more serious problem than a simple skin infection. Treating it like a routine abrasion or assuming no special antibiotic coverage is needed ignores both the organism profile and the risk of deep structure involvement.

quiz.q: A patient caught his hand in a high-pressure grease gun. The entry wound on the fingertip is a tiny pinhole and the finger feels only mildly sore one hour later. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Call hand surgery immediately, splint and elevate the finger, give tetanus and antibiotics, and avoid a digital block
Irrigate the pinhole vigorously in the department and observe for four hours before deciding
Reassure the patient and discharge with routine wound care since the wound looks minor
Perform a digital nerve block, then discharge with oral antibiotics and a follow-up in a week
quiz.why: High-pressure injection injuries look deceptively trivial at the entry point while material has already tracked along tendon sheaths, with an amputation rate approaching 30 to 48% if not treated as a surgical emergency. Hand surgery is called immediately; a digital block is specifically avoided because it raises pressure in an already swelling finger. Discharge, routine irrigation, or watching and waiting all squander the early window when intervention still has a chance to save the digit.

quiz.q: A child's forearm laceration was caused by a shattered wine glass. The wound edges look clean on inspection. What imaging step is indicated?
choices: None, since the wound looks clean on visual inspection
Plain film x-ray, because glass fragments larger than about 2 mm are usually radiopaque
Ultrasound only, since glass does not show on plain film
CT scan is mandatory regardless of wound appearance
quiz.why: Glass is radiopaque, and fragments larger than about 2 mm are visible on plain film most of the time, so any wound caused by glass gets an x-ray even when it looks clean, since appearance does not reliably predict retained fragments. Ultrasound is the better tool for radiolucent material like wood or plastic, not glass, and a full CT is not the routine first step for a straightforward laceration.

quiz.q: A patient has a laceration over the palm. To specifically test the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon, what should the examiner do?
choices: Ask the patient to extend the wrist against resistance
Ask the patient to spread the fingers against resistance
Hold the proximal interphalangeal joint straight and ask the patient to bend the fingertip
Hold all other fingers straight and ask the patient to make a full fist
quiz.why: The FDP is tested by holding the middle joint (PIP) straight and asking the patient to bend the fingertip (DIP), which isolates the deep flexor tendon. Making a full fist involves multiple tendons and does not isolate FDP, wrist extension against resistance tests wrist extensors rather than a finger flexor, and spreading the fingers against resistance tests the ulnar nerve's intrinsic muscles, not a flexor tendon.

quiz.q: A patient has a deep laceration on the palm with brisk bleeding from one visible vessel. A resident reaches for a hemostat to clamp it. What should happen instead?
choices: A tourniquet should be applied above the elbow before any exploration
The wound should be irrigated vigorously to stop the bleeding
Clamping is correct and should proceed immediately
Direct pressure and elevation should be used instead, because digital nerves run alongside the arteries and a blind clamp risks taking both
quiz.why: Clamping a bleeding vessel in the hand risks grabbing the adjacent digital nerve, since nerves run right alongside the arteries in that region — direct pressure and elevation control essentially every hand bleed without that risk. A proximal tourniquet is an overcorrection for a controllable local bleed, and irrigation does not address active bleeding at all.

quiz.q: A clean laceration to the cheek occurs at 10 pm; the patient is not seen until 8 am the next morning, roughly 10 hours later. Why might this face wound still reasonably be closed primarily despite the delay?
choices: Because the face and scalp are richly vascular and are commonly closed up to 24 hours after injury
Because timing does not matter for any wound location
Because facial wounds are always closed regardless of contamination or time
Because 10 hours exceeds the golden period and the wound must be left open
quiz.why: The face and scalp have a rich blood supply, which is why they are commonly closed up to 24 hours after injury even though extremity wounds have a shorter practical window. Timing does matter, it is just weighed alongside contamination, mechanism and blood supply rather than being an absolute cutoff, and facial wounds are not closed automatically regardless of how dirty or old they are.

quiz.q: Which of the following wound features would most strongly favor primary closure rather than delayed closure or leaving the wound open?
choices: A bite wound to the hand
A clean, linear incision less than 6 hours old with well-approximated edges and no contamination
A heavily contaminated crush wound with visible dead tissue
A puncture wound from a nail
quiz.why: A clean, linear, minimally contaminated wound seen soon after injury with edges that come together well is the classic candidate for primary closure. Punctures, hand and other high-risk bites, and contaminated crush wounds with dead tissue are all specifically listed as wounds that heal better left open or closed on a delay, because primary closure of a dirty wound traps infection inside.

quiz.q: A clinician wants to reduce the pain of a lidocaine injection for a laceration repair. Which combination of techniques is correct?
choices: Use topical LET on adults instead of injectable anesthesia for all wound types
Inject cold solution quickly through intact skin with a large-gauge needle
Buffer the lidocaine with sodium bicarbonate, warm it, use a small-gauge needle, and inject through the wound edges slowly
Skip buffering and inject as fast as possible to minimize total procedure time
quiz.why: Buffering with sodium bicarbonate raises the pH toward physiologic and reduces the sting, warming the solution and using a small (27 or 30 gauge) needle reduce discomfort further, and injecting through the wound edges rather than intact skin avoids a second painful puncture — all done slowly rather than rapidly. Cold solution, large-gauge needles and rapid injection all increase pain, and topical LET, while useful especially in children, is not a blanket substitute for injectable anesthesia in all wound types.

quiz.q: A physician is repairing a facial laceration in a cosmetically sensitive area and wants a suture that will be removed early to minimize scarring. Which suture size and removal timeframe fits the face?
choices: 3-0, removed in 7 to 10 days
4-0, removed in 10 to 14 days
No sutures are used on the face; only adhesive strips are appropriate
6-0, removed in 3 to 5 days
quiz.why: Facial wounds use fine 6-0 suture removed early, at 3 to 5 days, which minimizes both the tension marks from the stitches themselves and visible scarring in a cosmetically important area. 3-0 and longer removal times are used for tougher, less visible areas like the scalp or trunk, and sutures are absolutely still used on the face — adhesive strips are for tension-free, superficial wounds or reinforcement, not a universal substitute.

quiz.q: A 50 kg patient is to receive plain 1% lidocaine for a wound repair. Approximately how many milligrams is the maximum safe dose?
choices: About 225 mg
About 500 mg
There is no weight-based limit for plain lidocaine
About 45 mg
quiz.why: Plain lidocaine's maximum dose is 4.5 mg/kg, so for a 50 kg patient that is roughly 225 mg (well under the absolute ceiling of 300 mg). A dose of only 45 mg vastly underestimates the safe ceiling, 500 mg exceeds even the absolute maximum for plain lidocaine, and there is in fact a well-defined weight-based limit precisely because local anesthetic toxicity is dose-dependent.

quiz.q: A nurse is preparing to irrigate a laceration and reaches for a bottle of povidone-iodine to pour directly into the open wound. What is the concern with this plan?
choices: There is no concern; povidone-iodine is the preferred irrigant for open wounds
Povidone-iodine, along with hydrogen peroxide and alcohol, is toxic to the fibroblasts doing the healing and should stay on intact skin around the wound, not inside it
Povidone-iodine should be used only on facial wounds
Povidone-iodine is fine as long as it is diluted with saline first
quiz.why: Povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide and alcohol are all toxic to fibroblasts, the cells responsible for wound healing, so none of them belong inside the wound itself — they are reserved for prepping intact skin around it. Preferring it as an irrigant, restricting the concern to facial wounds only, or assuming dilution solves the toxicity all misstate the actual reason these agents are avoided inside the wound.

quiz.q: A patient has a short, clean, linear 1.5 cm laceration on the forearm with edges that fall together easily and no tension. Which closure method is well suited to this wound?
choices: Staples, because they are fastest for any forearm wound
Deep absorbable sutures only, bypassing any surface closure
Tissue adhesive, painted across the approximated skin edges
A pressure dressing alone with no closure
quiz.why: A short, clean, linear, low-tension wound with edges that already sit together is the textbook indication for tissue adhesive, painted across the closed surface rather than dripped into the wound. Staples are reasonable for some forearm wounds but are not specifically better suited here than adhesive for a wound this small and tension-free; skipping surface closure to only place deep sutures ignores that deep sutures are for taking tension off skin, not a substitute for skin closure; and a pressure dressing alone leaves a gaping wound unclosed.

quiz.q: A patient's laceration was repaired two days ago and pain, which had been improving, now begins to worsen again with new redness around the wound. What does this pattern most likely represent?
choices: An allergic reaction to the suture material requiring no further workup
A sign that the wound needs to be immediately reopened without examination
Normal healing; pain commonly worsens transiently on day two for no concerning reason
The earliest sign of wound infection, since infections often declare themselves and worsening pain after improvement is an early clue
quiz.why: Pain that is improving and then gets worse, especially with new redness, is described as the earliest useful signal of wound infection, and most wound infections declare themselves in the 2 to 5 day window. This is not normal expected healing, an unevaluated suture allergy is a less likely and less dangerous explanation to jump to first, and the correct next step is examination and a management decision, not reflexively reopening the wound without assessment.

quiz.q: A patient with an unknown tetanus vaccination history sustains a heavily contaminated wound from a farm injury. What is required?
choices: Vaccine and tetanus immune globulin 250 units IM, because an unknown or fewer-than-3-dose history with a dirty wound requires both
No intervention is needed unless the wound becomes visibly infected
Immune globulin alone, without vaccine
Vaccine only, since an unknown history is treated the same as a fully vaccinated patient
quiz.why: An unknown vaccination history is treated the same as fewer than 3 documented doses, and for a dirty wound that combination requires both the vaccine and tetanus immune globulin 250 units IM, since the patient may have no existing protection at all. Treating unknown history as fully vaccinated, withholding treatment until infection appears, or giving immune globulin without the vaccine all leave a gap in either immediate or lasting protection.

quiz.q: A healthy, currently vaccinated pet cat that is available for observation bites a child. What is the appropriate approach regarding rabies?
choices: Begin post-exposure prophylaxis immediately regardless of the animal's status
Observe the animal for 10 days; if it remains healthy, no rabies treatment is needed
Euthanize the animal immediately to test for rabies before deciding
No action is needed since cats cannot transmit rabies
quiz.why: A healthy, available dog, cat or ferret is observed for 10 days, and if it stays well throughout, no rabies treatment is needed, since a rabid animal would become symptomatic and die within that window. Starting prophylaxis immediately skips this well-established observation option, immediate euthanasia to test is not the standard approach for an available, currently healthy pet, and cats are absolutely capable of transmitting rabies, unlike small rodents which essentially never do.

quiz.q: A patient develops spreading, non-purulent cellulitis of the leg with no drainable collection on exam. Which antibiotic approach is most appropriate as a first-line choice?
choices: No treatment, since cellulitis resolves without antibiotics
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, assuming MRSA coverage is always required
Cephalexin or a penicillin, since non-purulent cellulitis is usually streptococcal
Incision and drainage, since all skin infections need a procedure
quiz.why: Non-purulent cellulitis, without an abscess to drain, is usually caused by streptococcus and treated with cephalexin or a penicillin rather than broad MRSA coverage, which is reserved for purulent presentations. Incision and drainage is the treatment for a drainable abscess, not for cellulitis with no collection, and untreated cellulitis can progress and does require antibiotics rather than watchful waiting alone.

quiz.q: A woman wakes up to find a bat flying in the bedroom where her toddler was sleeping. No bite marks are found on the child. How should this exposure be handled?
choices: The bat should simply be released outside and the family reassured
Only an adult witnessing direct contact with the bat would count as an exposure
No action needed, since there is no visible bite
Treated as a rabies exposure regardless of a visible bite, because a bat in the room of a sleeping or very young person counts as an exposure
quiz.why: A bat found in the room of a sleeping or very young person is treated as a rabies exposure even without a visible bite, because bat bites can be too small to see and a young child cannot reliably report contact. Assuming no action is needed because no bite is visible, simply releasing the bat, or requiring witnessed direct adult contact all underestimate the risk in exactly the population this rule is designed to protect.

quiz.q: A burn appears mottled red and white, has blisters, is drier than a superficial partial-thickness burn, and sensation is reduced but not absent. What depth is this, and does it count toward TBSA for fluid calculations?
choices: Deep partial-thickness burn; included in TBSA
Full-thickness burn; excluded from TBSA
Superficial partial-thickness burn; excluded from TBSA
Superficial burn; excluded from TBSA
quiz.why: Mottled red and white color, blisters, a drier appearance and reduced (but not absent) sensation describe a deep partial-thickness burn, which is included in the TBSA calculation used for fluid resuscitation, since only partial and full-thickness burn counts. A superficial burn has no blisters, a full-thickness burn is insensate rather than merely reduced, and any partial or full-thickness burn is included in TBSA, not excluded, so pairing this depth with exclusion is wrong.

quiz.q: A fire victim arrives with a pulse oximeter reading of 99% on room air after being pulled from a burning building. How should this oxygen saturation reading be interpreted?
choices: It reliably confirms adequate oxygenation and no further workup is needed
It may be falsely normal because the pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin; 100% oxygen and a co-oximetry level are needed
It means carbon monoxide poisoning has been ruled out
The reading should be repeated in 30 minutes before taking any action
quiz.why: In carbon monoxide poisoning, the pulse oximeter reads falsely normal because it cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so a 99% reading in a fire victim means essentially nothing about true oxygenation. The correct response is 100% oxygen and a co-oximetry level that specifically measures carboxyhemoglobin, not reassurance, not ruling out CO poisoning based on pulse ox, and not simply waiting to recheck the same unreliable number.

quiz.q: A patient has a full-thickness burn covering 3% of the forearm, with no other injuries. Does this meet burn center referral criteria?
choices: Only if there is also an inhalation injury present
No, because it is under 10% of body surface area
Yes, because any full-thickness burn at any age meets referral criteria regardless of size
Only if the patient is under 18 or over 65
quiz.why: Any full-thickness burn, at any age, meets American Burn Association referral criteria regardless of its total size, so a small 3% full-thickness burn still qualifies. The 10% threshold applies specifically to partial-thickness burns, not full-thickness ones, age alone is not the deciding factor here, and an inhalation injury is its own separate referral criterion, not a requirement layered on top of a full-thickness burn.

quiz.q: A patient has a circumferential full-thickness burn of the forearm. Over several hours, Doppler signals in the fingers become fainter and sensation is dropping. What is the appropriate procedure, and how does it differ from a fasciotomy?
choices: Amputation is required immediately given the vascular findings
No procedure is needed as long as a pulse can still be palpated
Fasciotomy, which is the same procedure as an escharotomy
Escharotomy, an incision through the full thickness of the dead skin only, which is more superficial than a fasciotomy that cuts into the fascia for compartment syndrome
quiz.why: A circumferential full-thickness burn forms a rigid eschar that constricts the swelling limb like a tourniquet, and the treatment is an escharotomy — an incision through the full thickness of the dead skin only. This is a distinct, more superficial procedure than a fasciotomy, which cuts deeper into the fascia and treats compartment syndrome from a different cause. Escharotomy and fasciotomy are not the same procedure, amputation is not the first-line response to worsening distal perfusion under an eschar, and waiting for pulselessness before acting risks losing the limb.

quiz.q: A patient has small, intact blisters under about 6 mm from a scald burn. What is the generally appropriate approach to these blisters?
choices: They are usually left alone, while large, tense blisters or those over joints are more commonly debrided
Aspirate the fluid with a needle but leave the blister roof intact
Apply silver sulfadiazine directly under the intact blister before doing anything else
Deroof them all immediately to inspect the wound bed
quiz.why: Small intact blisters under about 6 mm are usually left alone, since the intact skin serves as a natural biologic dressing, while larger, tense blisters, those over joints, or those certain to rupture are the ones commonly debrided — though this varies by protocol. Deroofing every blister regardless of size is not the standard approach, and injecting anything under an intact blister without a clear indication is not the described first step.

quiz.q: A radiograph report describes a fracture's displacement and angulation. By convention, these are described relative to which fragment?
choices: The proximal fragment
The distal fragment
Whichever fragment is larger
The fragment closest to the joint
quiz.why: Displacement and angulation are always described by what the distal fragment is doing relative to the proximal one, which is the fixed convention that keeps fracture descriptions consistent between providers. Describing it by the proximal fragment, by whichever fragment happens to be larger, or by proximity to a joint are not the standard, and using an inconsistent reference point would make handoffs ambiguous.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand and the elbow x-ray shows no obvious fracture line, but a posterior fat pad sign is present. How should this finding be interpreted?
choices: It indicates a chronic, old injury rather than an acute one
It is a normal variant in children and can be ignored
It is always abnormal and should be treated as an occult fracture, most often a supracondylar fracture at this age
It only matters if the anterior fat pad is also visible
quiz.why: A posterior fat pad sign is always abnormal, and in a child at this classic age it points to an occult supracondylar fracture even when no fracture line is directly visible, so the child is treated and immobilized accordingly. It is never dismissed as a normal variant, its significance does not depend on also seeing an anterior fat pad, and it is a marker of an acute elbow joint effusion, not specifically a chronic injury.

quiz.q: A patient fell on a flexed wrist and has a distal radius fracture displaced toward the palm. What is this injury called, and how does it differ from a Colles fracture?
choices: Colles fracture; Smith fractures do not exist
Galeazzi fracture; Colles involves the ulna instead of the radius
Boxer's fracture; Colles involves the wrist rather than the hand
Smith fracture; it is the reverse of Colles, which is dorsally displaced from a fall on an outstretched hand
quiz.why: A Smith fracture is a distal radius fracture displaced toward the palm from a fall on a flexed wrist, the reverse mechanism and displacement direction of a Colles fracture, which is dorsally displaced from a fall on an outstretched hand. Smith fractures are a real, named entity, Galeazzi is a completely different injury involving the distal radioulnar joint, and a boxer's fracture is a metacarpal neck fracture, unrelated to the wrist.

quiz.q: A patient has a mallet finger from a forced bend at the fingertip. What is the correct splinting approach, and what must never happen during care?
choices: Splint in continuous extension for 6 to 8 weeks; the joint must never be allowed to bend, even during splint changes
No splinting is needed; the tendon heals on its own with normal use
Splint in extension for only 3 days, then resume normal use
Splint in flexion for 2 weeks; the joint may bend briefly during splint changes
quiz.why: Mallet finger is an extensor tendon avulsion treated with continuous extension splinting for 6 to 8 weeks, and the joint must never be allowed to bend even momentarily during splint changes, because any flexion resets the tendon healing process. Flexion splinting is the opposite of correct treatment, skipping splinting entirely allows the deformity to become permanent, and 3 days is far too short a duration for the tendon to heal.

quiz.q: A patient with a clavicle fracture has skin over the fracture site that is visibly tented and appears about to break through. How urgently should orthopedics be involved compared to a routine middle-third clavicle fracture?
choices: No different urgency; sling and routine follow-up are appropriate either way
This is one of the situations that warrants ortho evaluation now, unlike most clavicle fractures which go into a sling for early motion
This should be managed exactly like an open fracture with antibiotics but no ortho involvement
Tented skin over a clavicle fracture is not a clinical concern
quiz.why: Tented skin that looks about to break through is specifically called out as a reason to involve ortho now, along with open fracture, neurovascular compromise, or more than about 2 cm of shortening, whereas most clavicle fractures — including the common middle-third break — go into a sling with early motion and routine follow-up. Treating it identically to routine cases ignores the imminent skin breakdown risk, and while antibiotics might eventually matter if the skin does break, orthopedic involvement is still required, not skipped.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old fell and has a shortened, externally rotated right leg. She cannot lift her heel off the bed and groin pain is reproduced with axial load on the heel. What is this presentation classic for?
choices: Compartment syndrome of the thigh
A simple ankle sprain
A hip fracture
A Lisfranc injury
quiz.why: Shortening and external rotation of the leg, inability to lift the heel (a positive straight leg raise test), and pain with axial loading on the heel are the classic triad for a hip fracture in an older adult after a low-energy fall. An ankle sprain would not shorten or externally rotate the whole leg, a Lisfranc injury is a midfoot problem with plantar bruising, and compartment syndrome presents with escalating pain and pain on passive stretch in a swollen limb, not this position and loading pattern.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old inverted his ankle playing basketball. He has tenderness limited to the anterior talofibular ligament, no tenderness over either malleolus, and he can bear weight and walk without difficulty. Do the Ottawa ankle rules recommend an x-ray?
choices: Yes, because ligament tenderness alone always triggers imaging
The Ottawa rules do not apply to sports injuries
Yes, any ankle injury requires imaging by the Ottawa rules
No, because there is no malleolar tenderness and he can bear weight, so imaging is not indicated by the rule
quiz.why: The Ottawa ankle rules call for imaging only when there is pain in the malleolar zone plus bony tenderness at the malleoli or inability to bear weight for four steps; isolated ligament tenderness with no malleolar bone tenderness and normal weight bearing does not meet the rule, so imaging is not indicated. Requiring imaging for every ankle injury defeats the purpose of the rule, ligament tenderness alone is exactly the finding the rule is designed to let you skip imaging for, and the rules are validated for and commonly applied to sports-related ankle injuries in alert adults.

quiz.q: A patient jumps from a height and lands on both heels, sustaining bilateral calcaneus fractures. What additional area of the skeleton should specifically be evaluated, and roughly how often is it involved?
choices: The lumbar spine for a burst fracture, in about 10% of cases
The skull, in nearly all cases
No additional evaluation is needed beyond the feet
The cervical spine, in about 50% of cases
quiz.why: Axial loading transmitted up the skeleton from a fall onto the heels causes an associated lumbar burst fracture in about 10% of cases, which is why the lumbar spine is specifically evaluated alongside bilateral calcaneus fractures. The cervical spine and skull are not the classically associated sites for this particular axial-load mechanism, and skipping additional evaluation would miss a clinically significant minority of patients with a second serious injury.

quiz.q: A patient has a grade III ankle sprain — a completely torn ligament with gross instability. Compared to a grade II sprain, how does the pain typically compare?
choices: Grade III is always far more painful than grade II
Grade III is often less painful than grade II, because a completely torn ligament has no intact fibers left to hurt
Pain is identical between grades and cannot be used to distinguish them
Grade III sprains are painless and asymptomatic
quiz.why: A completely torn ligament (grade III) often hurts less than a partially torn one (grade II), because there are no remaining intact fibers to generate pain — this is exactly why pain is a poor guide to severity in ligament injuries and stability must be tested directly. Assuming grade III is always more painful, that pain cannot differentiate at all, or that grade III is entirely painless all overstate or understate this counterintuitive but real pattern.

quiz.q: A patient has an ankle fracture with the fibular break located above the level of the joint line (the ankle mortise). Using the Weber classification, what does this suggest about stability?
choices: It means the fracture is definitely a Maisonneuve injury
It is almost always stable and can be treated with a simple boot
It suggests disruption of the syndesmosis and is typically unstable
Fibular fracture location above the joint has no bearing on stability
quiz.why: In the Weber system, a fibular fracture above the joint line disrupts the syndesmosis and is typically unstable, in contrast to a fracture below the line, which is usually stable. Calling it stable inverts the actual relationship, fracture location by definition determines the Weber classification and thus bearing on stability, and while a high fibular fracture raises suspicion for a Maisonneuve injury (which pairs it with a proximal fibula fracture and medial ankle injury), this alone does not confirm that specific diagnosis without further exam and imaging.

quiz.q: A patient with an open tibia fracture arrives in the department. According to Gustilo-Anderson grading, what wound size and soft tissue picture defines a Grade II open fracture?
choices: Over 10 cm with bone still coverable
Arterial injury requiring repair
Under 1 cm, clean wound
1 to 10 cm, with moderate soft tissue damage
quiz.why: Gustilo-Anderson Grade II is defined by a wound between 1 and 10 cm with moderate soft tissue damage, sitting between the minor Grade I (under 1 cm, clean) and the more severe Grade III subtypes. Under 1 cm and clean describes Grade I, over 10 cm with coverable bone describes Grade IIIA, and arterial injury requiring repair describes Grade IIIC — each is a distinct grade with its own implications for management and prognosis.

quiz.q: An open fracture wound is being repeatedly uncovered so several team members can each take a look. What is the concern with this practice, and what should be done instead?
choices: Repeated uncovering increases contamination risk; the wound should be photographed once, then covered with saline-moistened gauze
The wound should be left fully uncovered until orthopedics arrives
Each inspection should include fresh irrigation to offset contamination risk
There is no concern; repeated inspection improves documentation
quiz.why: Repeatedly uncovering an open fracture wound is exactly how it becomes contaminated in the department, so the correct approach is to photograph the wound once and then cover it with saline-moistened sterile gauze and a dry dressing so it is not disturbed again. Leaving it fully uncovered increases exposure time to airborne and contact contamination, and the department's role is removing only gross debris, not performing repeated irrigation, which is deliberately deferred to the operating room.

quiz.q: A patient with an open fracture is going to receive antibiotics. Within what timeframe of arrival should the first dose be given?
choices: Antibiotics are not indicated until culture results return
Within 1 hour
Within 6 hours
Within 24 hours, timed with the operative washout
quiz.why: Antibiotics for an open fracture are given within one hour of arrival, since the wound has been exposed to the environment from the moment of injury and the infection clock is already running. Waiting 6 or 24 hours, or waiting for cultures before starting empiric therapy, all needlessly delay a time-sensitive intervention that is meant to start immediately on presentation, well before the operative washout occurs.

quiz.q: A patient with a tibial fracture in a fresh cast develops escalating pain over several hours, unrelieved by opioids, with pain worsened by passively extending the toes. Which finding, if present, would be the LEAST reliable reason to rule out compartment syndrome?
choices: Pain reproduced with passive stretch of the compartment muscles
Escalating analgesic requirement
Strong distal pulses being present
Pain out of proportion to the injury
quiz.why: Strong pulses are the least reliable reassurance against compartment syndrome, since compartment pressure exceeds small-vessel perfusion pressure long before it reaches arterial pressure — pulses are typically preserved until very late, if compartment syndrome even progresses that far before treatment. Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and an escalating analgesic requirement are all recognized early, more reliable indicators that point toward the diagnosis rather than away from it.

quiz.q: During a shoulder reduction, which nerve must be assessed both before and after the procedure, and how is its sensory function specifically tested?
choices: The median nerve, by testing the OK sign
The ulnar nerve, by testing sensation at the little fingertip
The radial nerve, by testing wrist extension
The axillary nerve, by testing sensation over the outer deltoid, the regimental badge patch
quiz.why: Shoulder dislocation and its reduction put the axillary nerve at risk, and it is checked by testing sensation over the outer deltoid, the so-called regimental badge patch area, along with the ability to contract the deltoid. Wrist extension tests the radial nerve, which is more relevant to humeral shaft fractures; the OK sign and little fingertip sensation test the median and ulnar nerves respectively, which are the nerves checked for hand lacerations, not shoulder dislocations.

quiz.q: A splint is being applied to a hand injury. What position should the hand be splinted in to avoid permanent stiffness?
choices: The position of safety: wrist extended 20 to 30 degrees, knuckles bent 70 to 90 degrees, finger joints nearly straight
Wrist flexed and knuckles fully extended
Whatever position is most comfortable for the patient at the moment
Flat, with the wrist and fingers fully extended
quiz.why: The hand is splinted in the position of safety — wrist extended 20 to 30 degrees, knuckles (MCP joints) bent 70 to 90 degrees, and the finger joints (PIP/DIP) nearly straight — because this position keeps the collateral ligaments at their longest and prevents them from tightening into a stiff, contracted hand. Splinting the hand flat is specifically called out as a way to stiffen it permanently, a flexed wrist with extended knuckles is not the correct position, and simply going by momentary comfort ignores the long-term functional consequence.

quiz.q: A patient with a new short leg splint asks how to shower. Which discharge instruction is correct?
choices: Remove the splint before showering and reapply afterward
Keep the splint dry using a plastic bag over it while showering
Soaking the splint briefly is fine as long as it air-dries afterward
Push a scratching tool down inside the splint if it feels itchy, then keep it dry
quiz.why: The correct instruction is to keep the splint dry, typically using a plastic bag over it during showering, since a wet or wrinkled layer against the skin causes breakdown. Removing and reapplying a splint is not something the patient should do themselves, soaking it and hoping it air-dries risks skin maceration and loosens the splint's integrity, and pushing anything down inside the splint to scratch is specifically warned against because it can injure or infect the skin underneath.

quiz.q: A patient reports that after a lower extremity splint was applied and they went home, they now have increasing pain, numbness, and pale, cold toes. What should this prompt?
choices: Elevating the leg above the heart and waiting 24 hours before deciding
Reassurance that this is normal swelling after a splint
Immediate return to the department, since these are compartment syndrome screening symptoms
Waiting until the scheduled follow-up appointment in a week
quiz.why: Increasing pain, numbness, and pale or cold toes are exactly the return precautions taught at discharge because they function as a compartment syndrome screening tool for a patient who has gone home before swelling peaks — this combination requires immediate return, not reassurance or watchful waiting. Waiting for a scheduled follow-up or simply elevating and waiting 24 hours both risk allowing a genuine emergency to progress toward irreversible muscle damage.

quiz.q: A patient is being fitted for a walker instead of crutches. Where should the handgrips be positioned, and how much elbow bend is appropriate?
choices: At shoulder height with arms fully extended
At hip level with elbows locked straight
Handgrip height does not matter for walkers, only for crutches
At the wrist creases with arms hanging at the sides, elbows bent 15 to 20 degrees
quiz.why: Walker handgrips are set at the wrist creases with the arms hanging naturally at the sides, giving about 15 to 20 degrees of elbow bend, which allows a stable, comfortable weight-bearing position. Shoulder-height grips or fully extended, locked elbows would force an awkward, unstable posture, and fit absolutely matters for a walker just as it does for crutches, since improper height affects both safety and comfort.

quiz.q: A 5-month-old, who is not yet walking, is brought in with a femur fracture reportedly from rolling off a couch. What should this combination of age and injury raise concern for?
choices: Possible non-accidental trauma, since any fracture in a non-ambulatory infant is a recognized red flag
A normal toddler's fracture pattern
A Salter-Harris type I fracture specific to this age
Nothing unusual; rolling injuries commonly cause femur fractures at this age
quiz.why: Any fracture in an infant who is not yet walking is specifically listed as a pattern with a high probability of inflicted injury, because the forces generated by a short fall from a couch are rarely sufficient to fracture a healthy femur in a pre-ambulatory infant. Treating it as an unremarkable rolling injury or a toddler's fracture (which occurs in children who have started walking) misses the red flag, and this scenario is not specifically a Salter-Harris pattern, which applies to growth plate injuries in general, not this age-and-mechanism combination.

quiz.q: A radiograph of a child's distal radius shows the metaphysis compressed and bulging without a clear fracture line through the cortex. What is this injury, and how is it typically treated?
choices: A greenstick fracture, requiring surgical fixation
A buckle (torus) fracture, treated with a removable wrist splint for about 3 weeks
A Salter-Harris type V injury requiring urgent orthopedic surgery
A toddler's fracture, requiring non-weight-bearing status
quiz.why: A buckle (torus) fracture is the soft, immature metaphysis compressing and bulging rather than breaking through, and it is a stable injury now typically treated with a removable wrist splint for about 3 weeks rather than a rigid cast. A greenstick fracture is a different pattern where one side of the bone bends while the other breaks, Salter-Harris V is a crush of the growth plate itself with a poor prognosis and is a different entity, and a toddler's fracture is a lower extremity tibial injury, unrelated to the wrist.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old was pulled up sharply by one hand, immediately stopped using the arm, and now holds it slightly bent and turned palm-down with no swelling or deformity. What is the expected timeline for the child to use the arm again after appropriate reduction?
choices: The arm requires 3 weeks of splinting before use resumes
Immediately, within seconds, with no observation needed
Within about 5 to 30 minutes of reduction
Not for 24 to 48 hours, since healing takes time
quiz.why: Nursemaid's elbow is reduced with a quick maneuver, and the child typically resumes using the arm within about 5 to 30 minutes as the radial head slips back under its ligament — this return-to-function timeline is part of confirming the diagnosis was correct. Expecting instant, symptom-free use with zero observation ignores that some settling time is normal, a 24 to 48 hour delay would suggest the reduction did not work or the diagnosis is wrong, and this injury does not involve a fracture, so it needs no prolonged splinting.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old with several days of back pain reports new numbness in the area where he would sit on a saddle, along with bilateral leg weakness. What does this combination of findings specifically suggest, and what test result would further support it?
choices: A simple L5 radiculopathy affecting one leg
A Salter-Harris fracture of the spine
Ordinary mechanical back pain; reassurance and early movement are appropriate
Cauda equina syndrome; reduced rectal tone and urinary retention would further support the diagnosis
quiz.why: Saddle anesthesia combined with bilateral leg symptoms is a classic cauda equina picture, and finding reduced rectal tone or urinary retention on further exam would reinforce that diagnosis and the need for urgent MRI and surgery. This is not ordinary mechanical back pain given these red-flag findings, a unilateral L5 radiculopathy would not explain bilateral symptoms and saddle anesthesia, and Salter-Harris classification applies to pediatric growth plate fractures, not adult back pain.

quiz.q: A worried parent asks why a bruise pattern of multiple fractures at different stages of healing, found incidentally on imaging, is concerning. What is the correct explanation, and what is the legal obligation in New Jersey?
choices: It is a pattern with high concern for inflicted injury; any person with reasonable cause to suspect abuse must report it to the State Central Registry
Only a physician, never a technician or nurse, is legally required to report suspected abuse in New Jersey
The family should be asked to explain before any report is made, and a report is only filed if the explanation is unsatisfactory
It is a normal finding in active toddlers and requires no action
quiz.why: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing is one of the patterns carrying high concern for inflicted injury, and New Jersey law requires any person with reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused to report it to the State Central Registry — proof or certainty is not required, and deciding whether abuse actually occurred is not the reporter's job. This is not a normal incidental finding to wave off, the reporting duty in New Jersey applies broadly to any person, not physicians only, and reporting is not conditioned on first getting an explanation from the family or judging it unsatisfactory.

quiz.q: A wound resulting from a controlled bowel resection during surgery, with no gross contamination, best fits which contamination class and its associated infection risk?
choices: Clean, about 1 to 2%
Clean-contaminated, about 5 to 10%
Contaminated, about 10 to 20%
Dirty, over 25%
quiz.why: A controlled entry into the gut, even without spillage, is by definition clean-contaminated, carrying an infection risk of about 5 to 10%, higher than a purely clean wound made under fully sterile conditions with no entry into a colonized body cavity. Calling it clean ignores that the bowel lumen is not sterile, and contaminated or dirty categories are reserved for fresh traumatic or grossly soiled wounds, not a controlled surgical entry.

quiz.q: A patient has a laceration at the base of the ring finger. He can flex the fingertip normally but cannot bend the middle joint when the other fingers are held straight. Which structure is most likely injured?
choices: The extensor tendon
The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon
The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon
The radial nerve
quiz.why: Normal fingertip flexion means the FDP is intact, but inability to bend the middle joint when the other fingers are isolated and held straight — the specific FDS test — points to an FDS injury, since FDS is the tendon responsible for that isolated motion. The radial nerve does not control finger flexion tendons, and an extensor tendon injury would impair straightening the finger, not bending it.

quiz.q: A patient asks why topical LET is being applied to her child's forehead laceration instead of an injection. What is the correct explanation?
choices: LET is used because injectable anesthetics are not safe in children under any circumstances
LET works instantly, within seconds of application
LET is reserved only for wounds that will be closed with sutures, never adhesive
LET numbs the wound over 20 to 30 minutes and often avoids the need for an injection, making it a common first choice for children and facial wounds
quiz.why: Topical LET, soaked onto the wound for 20 to 30 minutes, often makes a painful injection unnecessary and is the standard first move for children and for face and scalp wounds specifically because of this. Injectable anesthetics are used safely in children when needed, so LET is not a strict safety requirement, it does not work instantly and needs its full soak time, and it is not limited only to wounds that end up sutured.

quiz.q: A patient asks how long she should wait to be rechecked after a high-risk hand wound was repaired, given that most infections have not yet declared themselves at discharge. What is the standard recheck interval?
choices: 48 hours
One week
One month
24 hours
quiz.why: High-risk wounds are scheduled for a recheck at 48 hours specifically because most wound infections declare themselves in the 2 to 5 day window, and 48 hours catches early infection while it is still manageable. 24 hours may be too early to see a developing infection, and a week or a month would allow a serious infection to progress significantly before it is caught.

quiz.q: A patient with facial burns, singed nasal hair, and a hoarse voice from an enclosed-space fire is being evaluated. What should be prioritized before anything else?
choices: Wound dressing selection
Early airway management, since these signs suggest impending airway swelling and intubation should happen while it is still possible
Determining burn center referral criteria
Calculating total body surface area burned
quiz.why: Singed nasal hair, a hoarse voice, and facial burns from an enclosed-space fire are airway red flags, and the priority is early intubation while it is still anatomically possible, before swelling closes the airway. Dressing selection, referral criteria and TBSA calculation are all real and necessary steps, but none of them take priority over securing an airway that is actively at risk of closing.

quiz.q: A patient has snuffbox tenderness after a fall but a normal wrist x-ray. Why is this treated as a scaphoid fracture despite the negative imaging, and what determines the urgency?
choices: Because a normal x-ray with tenderness always means a soft tissue sprain, not a fracture
Because the scaphoid has no notable blood supply concerns and the concern is purely cosmetic
Because scaphoid fractures can be invisible on initial x-ray, and its blood supply enters from the far end, so a fracture near that end risks avascular necrosis if missed
Because all wrist tenderness after a fall is treated identically regardless of exam findings
quiz.why: Scaphoid fractures are notoriously invisible on initial imaging, and because the bone's blood supply enters from the distal end and runs backward, a fracture near the proximal end can cut off that supply and lead to avascular necrosis if it is dismissed as a sprain. Treating all wrist tenderness the same regardless of exam location ignores the specific significance of snuffbox tenderness, assuming a normal x-ray rules out fracture is exactly the trap this teaching point warns against, and the vascular risk is a real functional concern, not merely cosmetic.

quiz.q: A patient has a knee injury with gross instability suggesting a knee dislocation that reduced spontaneously before arrival. Why is this injury treated as limb-threatening even though the joint now looks aligned?
choices: Because the patella is always fractured in this injury
Because this injury only threatens sensation, not blood supply
Because knee dislocations always require immediate amputation
Because of the risk of popliteal artery injury, which can be assessed using the ankle-brachial index
quiz.why: Knee dislocation is limb-threatening because of the risk of popliteal artery injury, and since many dislocations reduce on their own before the patient is even seen, the diagnosis rests on a history of gross instability plus vascular assessment — an ankle-brachial index under 0.9 prompts CT angiography regardless of how the joint looks on exam. Amputation is not an automatic outcome, a patella fracture is not a defining feature of this specific injury, and the primary threat is vascular (arterial), not merely sensory.

quiz.q: Why is elevating a limb above heart level the wrong move when compartment syndrome is suspected, in contrast to typical swelling management?
choices: Elevation lowers the arterial pressure driving blood into the compartment, which can worsen perfusion; the limb should be kept at heart level instead
Elevation has no effect on compartment pressure either way
Elevation is wrong only if the patient also has an open fracture
Elevation is always correct and should be done as high as possible
quiz.why: For most swelling, elevation helps by promoting venous and lymphatic drainage, but in suspected compartment syndrome it lowers the arterial pressure that is driving what blood flow remains into the already-compromised compartment, so the limb is instead kept at heart level while the cast and padding are split to skin. Assuming elevation is always beneficial ignores this specific exception, claiming no effect at all is incorrect, and this principle applies to suspected compartment syndrome generally, not only when an open fracture happens to be present.

quiz.q: During procedural sedation for a joint reduction, what equipment should be at the bedside before the sedation begins?
choices: Only a pulse oximeter is needed
Monitor, pulse oximetry, waveform capnography, oxygen, suction, a bag-valve mask, airway equipment and reversal agents
Just an IV line, since airway equipment is kept in a central supply room
A crash cart is only needed if the patient has a known cardiac history
quiz.why: Procedural sedation carries a real risk of respiratory depression, so full monitoring and airway rescue equipment — a monitor, pulse oximetry, waveform capnography, oxygen, suction, a bag-valve mask, airway equipment and reversal agents — must be at the bedside and ready before sedation starts, not fetched after a problem develops. Relying on pulse oximetry alone misses early hypoventilation that capnography catches sooner, keeping airway equipment in a separate room defeats the purpose of having it ready, and this preparation is standard for any sedation, not conditional on cardiac history alone.

quiz.q: A child's ankle x-ray shows a fracture line running through the physis and extending down into the epiphysis, entering the joint. Which Salter-Harris type is this, and why does joint involvement matter?
choices: Type II; this type never enters the joint
Type I; joint involvement is not a concern with this type
Type III; entering the joint raises concern for both growth disturbance and joint surface irregularity requiring precise alignment
Type V; this is the crush pattern
quiz.why: A fracture line through the physis and down into the epiphysis, entering the joint, is a Type III injury, and joint involvement matters because an irregular articular surface can cause long-term joint problems in addition to the usual growth plate risk, so precise alignment matters more than for a purely metaphyseal pattern. Type I runs straight through the physis without describing this epiphyseal extension, Type V is a crush injury with a different mechanism and appearance, and Type II by definition extends into the metaphysis rather than the epiphysis, so it is the wrong pairing here.
